T–S · Question 1 — M4 Activation
A visitor arrives at Vertex Logistics. They ask: "Excuse me — where's the cafeteria?" Give directions using prepositions of place: next to, in front of, behind, between, on the left/right. How would you answer?
S–S · Question 2 — Movement
Partner A: you're at the main entrance. Give 4 steps to reach the meeting room on floor 3. Partner B: draw the route on paper as they listen. Use: Go straight / Turn left or right / Take the elevator / It's on your left.
Class · Question 3 — Is there…?
Go around the room: each person answers "Is there a [place] in your building?" Use there is / there isn't. Include where it is: "Yes, there's a gym — it's on the ground floor, next to reception."
Teacher Note — Direction Errors to Watch
"Go to straight" ✗ → "Go straight" ✅. "In the left" ✗ → "On the left" ✅. "You turn right" ✗ → "Turn right" ✅ — imperative, no subject. Write on board, use in §5.
⚡ Quick Win — 20 seconds
Say out loud: "Go straight, turn left at the elevator, and it's on your right — next to the printer." — Four direction structures. One route. Twenty seconds.
5 min · 3 questions · Badge 🗺️ when done
§2
Speaking · Guided Tour of Vertex Logistics
3 rounds · Give directions · Describe locations · Handle problems on the tour
8–10 min
T–S
Scene: Reception, Vertex Logistics. A new supplier from Chicago just arrived. Ana is giving a quick tour. Describe the ground floor: where is reception, what's next to it, where's the elevator, and what's on the first floor.

"Welcome to Vertex! This is our reception area. The security desk is in front of the main entrance. The elevator is on the left — next to the stairs. The cafeteria is on the first floor. Go straight from the elevator — it's on your right."

there is/are + prepositions of place + imperative directions — M4 in full context

S–S
Floor 2 — Operations. Partner A: you're the visitor. You need to find: the meeting room, the IT office, and the printer. Partner B: give directions for each, using prepositions and imperatives. Switch after all three. Time: 60 seconds.

"The meeting room is at the end of the corridor, on your left. The IT office is between the meeting room and the break room. The printer? Go past the IT office and turn right — it's in front of the window."

at the end of · between · past · in front of · turn right — movement prepositions in action

Class
Problem during the tour. Something goes wrong — choose one: (a) the elevator is out of order, (b) the meeting room is full, (c) the visitor's badge doesn't work on floor 3. Report the problem using there is a problem with… / can't / need. Then say what to do instead.

"There's a problem — the elevator isn't working today. I'm sorry — we can't use it. We need to use the stairs. They're on the right, next to the fire exit. It's only two floors — not far!"

there is a problem + can't + need + preposition — M1+M4+M5 in one problem sentence

Teacher Note — M4 Prepositions of Movement vs Place
Students confuse "to/from/past/through" (movement) with "next to/in front of/behind" (static place). Quick test after Round 2: "Go through the door" — movement or place? "The door is next to the elevator" — movement or place? 30 seconds. Clarifies before §5 grammar focus.

Teacher Note — "past" vs "in front of"
"Go past the cafeteria" = you're moving, you pass it (movement). "The cafeteria is in front of the elevator" = describing a static position (place). This distinction is the core of M4 movement vocabulary and the most common error in guided tours. Drill with 3 examples of each.
🗣️ Micro-Speaking — 45 seconds
Give 4-step directions to somewhere in your real building — use at least 3 words from the list.
Model: "Go straight down the corridor, turn left at the corner, go past the printer, and it's opposite the stairs."

Teacher Note — Spin the Wheel
Project on screen. Student spins. They have 30 seconds to answer the prompt. Class votes: thumbs up if directions were clear, thumbs sideways if some errors, thumbs down if they got lost. No pressure — the game creates safe failure. Badge 🎡 after 5 spins total.
§4
Colloquial · 4 Phrases for Tours & Directions
Polite · helpful · professional — exactly what a tour guide sounds like
5 min
"This way, please."
The most useful tour phrase. Replaces long direction sentences when you're walking and can gesture. Professional and natural in any company context.
[Walking to meeting room] "This way, please — it's just around the corner."
"You can't miss it."
Classic ending to directions — tells the listener the destination is obvious once they arrive. Confident and reassuring.
"Turn right, and it's the big door at the end. You can't miss it!"
"It's just around the corner."
Tells someone a place is very close. "Just" minimizes the distance — polite and encouraging. Very natural in casual corporate English.
"Is the cafeteria far?" — "No — it's just around the corner!"
"Follow me — I'll show you."
When directions are too complex, this phrase saves the interaction. Very common in Mexican and US corporate environments. Shows initiative and hospitality.
"It's complicated — follow me, I'll show you."
Teacher Note — Tour Phrase Chain
Run the tour in 60 seconds: Teacher walks to door, student gives all 4 phrases in sequence — "This way please → just around the corner → you can't miss it → follow me I'll show you." Natural sequence. Repeat twice. Speed round.
§5
Grammar · Prepositions of Place & Movement — M4 Applied
Problem → Tool · Static vs moving · Imperatives for directions · Activities + Poll
10–12 min
🚨 Real Situation — Lost Supplier at Vertex
A supplier from Monterrey calls: "I'm at the main entrance but I can't find the meeting room on floor 3. Can you help me?"
You want to say: "Sube al tercer piso. Dobla a la izquierda. El salón está enfrente del elevador."
❓ How do you say this in English — imperatives + movement + place prepositions?
✅ Three Tools for Directions
Tool 1 — Imperative: No subject → "Go straight / Turn left / Take the elevator / Walk past the stairs"
Tool 2 — Movement prepositions: to / from / past / through / along / up / down
Tool 3 — Place prepositions (static): next to / in front of / behind / between / opposite / on the left/right
TypePrepositionExample at Vertex❌ Common error
Movement to / from / past / through "Go through the double doors, past the printer." "Go in the doors" ✗
Static place next to / opposite / between "The room is opposite the elevator." "The room is in front the elevator" ✗
Direction on the left / right · at the end "It's on your left, at the end of the corridor." "In the left" ✗ → ON the left ✅
Imperative Go / Turn / Take / Walk / Follow "Turn right, take the elevator to floor 3." "You turn right" ✗ — no subject
⚠️ Top 3 direction errors — correct every time:
✘ "Go to straight" → ✅ Go straight — no "to" with straight
✘ "In the left / In the right" → ✅ On the left / On the right — always ON
✘ "The room is in front the elevator" → ✅ in front OF the elevator — never drop "of"
⚡ Quick Poll — 3 Questions

✏️ Activity A — Choose the Correct Preposition
1. Go ___ the double doors — the meeting room is on the left.
2. The cafeteria is ___ the elevator — you can see it when you get out.
3. Walk ___ the printer and turn right at the corner.
4. The IT office is ___ the left, between the two meeting rooms.
🗣️ Micro-Speaking — 60 seconds
Give your partner real directions from your company's entrance to your desk — use at least 2 movement prepositions and 2 place prepositions. Partner listens and draws the route.
✏️ Activity B — True or False? Direction Rules
"Go to straight and turn left" — correct way to give directions.
"The printer is in front of the window" — correct use of "in front of."
"Turn right at the corner" — imperative, no subject — correct structure.
"The room is in the left" — correct preposition for location.
§6
Listening · Marcos Gives the Factory Tour
Directions + locations + problems + integration · Badge 🎧
8–10 min
Marcos Gives the Tour — Vertex Logistics, Celaya
A1.1 · M6 · S4A · Voice: ElevenLabs · Speed: 0.78
0:00 0:00

Good morning! My name is Marcos Ruiz — I'm the logistics coordinator here at Vertex Logistics in Celaya. Welcome to our facility! I'm going to give you a quick tour today.

So, we're starting here at the main entrance. This is our reception area — there are two receptionists at the desk. The security office is behind reception, on the left. Please sign in here first and get your visitor badge.

Now, follow me — this way, please. We're going to walk through the main corridor. On your right, you can see the cafeteria. It's between the reception and the IT department. The IT office is at the end of this corridor, opposite the stairs. Go past the cafeteria and turn left — you can't miss it.

Let's take the elevator to the third floor. Oh — there's a problem. The elevator isn't working today. We need to use the stairs. They're on your left, next to the fire exit. I'm sorry — it's only three floors. Not far!

Here we are — the operations floor! There are twelve workstations in this open space. My desk is in front of the window — the one on the right. The meeting rooms are behind us: Room A is on the left, Room B is on the right. They're opposite each other.

There's a break room at the end of the corridor — go straight and turn right. There's coffee, tea, and a microwave. It's small but very useful! And that's our tour. Any questions? The bathroom is just around the corner — you can't miss it!

📎 ElevenLabs: Voice — Marcos (American English) · Speed 0.78 · A1.1 M6 S4A · ~195 words · all direction structures integrated

Teacher Note — Map Drawing Task
Pre-listening: students draw a blank floor plan (rectangle with some squares). As they listen, they label: reception, cafeteria, IT office, stairs, elevator, meeting rooms A and B, break room. After: compare maps with partner. This turns listening into a spatial/visual exercise — retention doubles.
1. Where is the IT department?
2. Why do they use the stairs instead of the elevator?
3. True or False: Marcos's desk is in front of the window on the right.
4. True or False: Meeting Room A and Room B are next to each other.

Speaking Cards — Directions & Tour
6 scenarios · 30 seconds each · speak before you think
Card 1 / 6
CARD 1 OF 6
Give a visitor directions from the main entrance to your real desk. 4 steps. Use go / turn / past / on the left.
M4: imperative + movement + place prepositions
CARD 2 OF 6
Describe your building using there is / there are. Name 4 places and where each one is.
M4: "There's a cafeteria on the first floor, next to…"
CARD 3 OF 6
The elevator is broken. A visitor needs to reach floor 4. What do you tell them? Use can't + need + stairs directions.
M5+M4: "I'm sorry — we can't use the elevator. You need to…"
CARD 4 OF 6
Describe Marcos's tour from the listening — from memory. Where is the cafeteria? The IT office? The break room?
Listening recall: position words + corridor/floor references
CARD 5 OF 6
Give a 30-second mini-tour of your real company — or any building you know. Use at least 4 prepositions.
All M4: next to / opposite / at the end / through / past / on the left
CARD 6 OF 6 ⭐
You are Marcos. A new supplier calls — they're lost at the entrance. Give them full directions to the 3rd-floor meeting room by phone. No gestures allowed.
All M4 + colloquial: "This way… just around the corner… you can't miss it… follow me…"

✅ I Can Now… — Click each one when confident
I can give step-by-step directions using imperatives: Go / Turn / Take / Walk / Follow — no subject.
I know the difference: movement (through / past / along) vs place (next to / opposite / in front of).
I always say "ON the left/right" — never "in" or "at" the left.
I can handle a problem mid-tour: "I'm sorry — the elevator isn't working. We need to use the stairs."
I can give a real tour of my building or company in English — and it sounds natural.
"This way, please."
Use next time you walk someone anywhere in your building in English. One phrase replaces five sentences.
"Follow me — I'll show you."
When directions get complicated, use this. It shows initiative, hospitality, and confidence — all in 5 words.
"You can't miss it."
End every set of directions with this. It reassures the listener and sounds like a native — not a textbook.
